title: Blox: A Modular Toolkit for Deep Learning Schedulers
one_line: A modular Python toolkit that decomposes DL cluster schedulers into seven swappable abstractions (admission, scheduling, placement, launch, preemption, cluster management, metrics) so prior schedulers can be re-implemented, compared and composed on a common simulator and cluster runtime.

repo.evidence: https://github.com/msr-fiddle/blox is linked from the paper abstract and Section 1; repo/Readme.md:2 states 'This repository contains the source code implementation of the Eurosys 2024 paper Blox: A Modular Toolkit for Deep Learning Schedulers... done as part of Microsoft Research's Project Fiddle'. msr-fiddle is the authors' organisation (Amar Phanishayee, MSR). Repo contains the real system (blox/blox_manager.py, blox/cluster_state.py, blox/job_state.py, schedulers/, placement/, admission_control/, workload/, simulator_runner/), ~47.9k lines of Python, MIT licensed.
repo.badge_evidence: none found - web search of EuroSys '24 materials returned no Artifacts Available/Functional/Reproduced badge for this paper, and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3627703.3629583 returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so this is 'not found' rather than 'confirmed absent'.

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official implementation per repo/Readme.md:2 and the paper's abstract/Section 1 link. Contains the actual system, not a placeholder: core abstractions in blox/blox_manager.py, blox/cluster_state.py, blox/job_state.py; policies in schedulers/{fifo,las,srtf,optimus,tiresias,gavel,proportional}.py, placement/placement.py, admission_control/{accept_all,load_based_accept}.py; workload generation in workload/workload.py + workload/model_zoo.py; simulation drivers in simulator_runner/simulator.py and blox_examples/. Caveat: the Pollux, Themis and Synergy-Tune scheduling policies listed in the paper's Table 3 are NOT in the release (grep for pollux|themis across the tree yields only a comment at schedulers/optimus.py:31), so paper Figures 3, 5, 8, 9 have no code behind them.

H2_no_root.evidence: Simulation mode is two user-space Python processes communicating over localhost gRPC (simulator_runner/simulator.py:446, blox/blox_manager.py:44-47). No kernel module, eBPF, perf counter, KVM, /proc/sys write or hugepage anywhere on that path. blox/deployment/__init__.py is empty, so 'import blox' does not pull in the cluster-only deps 'numa' (blox/deployment/grpc_client_nm.py:5) or 'redis' (blox/deployment/node_data_relay.py:3). All 3 'sudo' and 42 'docker' red-flag hits are inside vendored NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples READMEs under workload_synergy/models/** (e.g. workload_synergy/models/deepspeech.pytorch/README.md:12) that are only used for real training runs; no Dockerfile is needed. The cluster-mode node manager only reads /proc/meminfo and /proc/driver/nvidia (blox/deployment/grpc_client_nm.py:68,95).

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: Section 4 states 'all our experiments in this section are simulations'. The 128-GPU cluster (32 servers x 4 V100) exists only as rows of a pandas dataframe registered over gRPC (simulator_simple.py:357-378 with number_of_machines=32, gpus_per_machine=4; blox/cluster_state.py:36-46). Cost is CPU + RAM only; 16 cores / 125 GB RAM is ample and --simulator-rpc-port (Readme.md:141-159) allows many configs in parallel. Concern: the real-cluster results - Figure 18 (32 GPUs on 8x p3.8xlarge, Section 7) and Figure 19 (lease renewal swept to 256 GPUs) - have no meaningful single-GPU scale-down and are out of reach on one A5000; they are not the paper's headline contribution, but any add-on that depends on them is infeasible here.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: Deps are five pip packages, all user-space (Readme.md:93-98): grpcio, grpcio-tools, matplotlib, pandas, numpy. Pins are stale but workable in a conda env: pandas must be <2.0 because blox/cluster_state.py:89 calls gpu_df.append (removed in pandas 2.0) and the README pins pandas==1.3.0, and protobuf must be <5 because blox/deployment/grpc_server_rm.py:42 passes including_default_value_fields=True; both force Python <=3.10 via conda rather than the system 3.12. gRPC stubs are gitignored (.gitignore:7) and must be generated with blox/deployment/Makefile. Data: the only external input is the Philly cluster_job_log, publicly downloadable from https://github.com/msr-fiddle/philly-traces as named in workload/parse_philly_jobs.py:14,33 (verified public; ~1 GB tar.gz, 6.6 GB extracted, fits the ~257 GB free). Per-model iteration-time/throughput profiles are committed as Python (workload/models/res18_1.py:11-29), so no model weights or extra datasets are needed for the simulated results. Pollux-Trace and Tiresias-Trace are public upstream but have no loader in the repo (workload/workload.py:90 references self.trace, never assigned).

reproduce.target: Figure 6 (page 6) - average JCT of FIFO vs Tiresias vs Optimus on Philly-Trace as load is swept 1 to 9 jobs/hour on 128 GPUs - supporting the paper's central 'revisiting' claim that above ~7 jobs/hour Tiresias has higher JCT than FIFO because preemption-heavy fair scheduling penalises long jobs. Figure 7 (responsiveness) comes free from the same run, since blox/blox_manager.py:277-288 writes the responsiveness JSON alongside the JCT JSON.
reproduce.scale_down: Sweep loads {1,3,5,7,9} instead of {1..9} (15 configs instead of 27, adding 6 and 8 only if the curves are close near the claimed crossover). Track jobs 3000-3200 via --start-job-track/--end-job-track for the first pass instead of 3000-4000 - the run terminates when all tracked jobs finish (blox/blox_manager.py:251), so this is the dominant runtime knob - then widen to 3000-4000 for the final numbers. Keep the cluster at 32x4 = 128 GPUs; shrinking it would change the claim. Run 8-12 configs concurrently on distinct ports (--simulator-rpc-port, Readme.md:141-159) across the 16 available cores.
reproduce.rationale: Arguing for H: the exact driver is committed and hardcoded - simulator_runner/simulator.py:430-445 encodes precisely the Figure 6/7 sweep (schedulers Tiresias/Optimus/Fifo, np.arange(1,10,1.0) loads, 32x4 GPUs, jobs 3000-4000) and blox_examples/blox_new_flow_multi_run.py:63-78 dispatches them; Readme_figure.md:4-16 gives the command pair. Pulling it down to M: (1) gRPC stubs are gitignored (.gitignore:7) and blox/deployment/Makefile writes into a grpc_stubs/ directory that does not exist, with no __init__.py; (2) stub import styles are mutually incompatible (simulator_simple.py:20 'from blox.deployment.grpc_stubs import rm_pb2' vs blox/deployment/grpc_server_rm.py:18 bare 'import rm_pb2' vs blox/deployment/grpc_client_rm.py:10 joining a file path as a directory), needing a PYTHONPATH fix; (3) README commands assume a flat layout that no longer exists (simulator.py is under simulator_runner/, blox_new_flow_multi_run.py under blox_examples/, and blox_examples/blox_new_flow_dynamic_policy.py:12 imports predict_simulation as top-level); (4) three stale pins (Python<=3.10, pandas<2, protobuf<5); (5) one of the three target schedulers crashes as released - blox/deployment/grpc_client_rm.py:268 reads self.optimus_scale_by_gpus which is commented out at lines 232-243; (6) the bundled plotter is broken - simulator_simple.py:182-287 expects filenames without the acceptance policy while blox/blox_manager.py:253 writes them with it, and line 281 references an undefined 'free_gpu' - so Figure 6 must be re-plotted from the emitted JSON; (7) the ~1 GB Philly trace must be fetched and parsed separately; (8) the README itself budgets 'around 8hrs' for one full sweep (Readme.md:110). Expect the reproduced Tiresias curve to track LAS rather than the paper's Tiresias, because schedulers/tiresias.py:42-52 computes the multi-queue discretized-LAS order and then discards it. No artifact badge was found to raise confidence.

addons.name: Preemption-cost-aware simulation and re-audit of the high-load conclusions
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that charging a per-job checkpoint/restore cost on every preemption in Blox's simulated progress model changes the FIFO/LAS/Tiresias/Optimus ranking on average JCT - and specifically narrows or reverses the paper's Tiresias-worse-than-FIFO crossover - at loads >= 6 jobs/hour on Philly-Trace, with the effect growing in checkpoint size and shrinking in round duration.
addons.mechanism: Make a job that was suspended in the previous round lose c(model, num_GPUs) seconds of the next round before making progress. blox/blox_manager.py:354 already sets active_jobs[jid]['suspended']=1 on preemption and :386 clears it on relaunch, so the signal exists; the progress update at blox/deployment/grpc_client_rm.py:251-264 simply has to consume it. Add ckpt_save_s / ckpt_restore_s fields to the ModelStats profile classes under workload/models/ and thread them onto jobs in workload/workload.py. Anchor the values by measuring torch.save/torch.load of the state dict plus dataloader warm-up for the zoo's models on the local A5000, then sweep 0-120 s. Report avg JCT, responsiveness and the preemption count already logged through utils.collect_custom_metrics(..., {'num_preemptions': ...}). Mirror the same cost into the synthesizer's lookahead at simulator_runner/predict_simulation.py:136-177 so the two progress models stay consistent.
addons.motivating_evidence: blox/deployment/grpc_client_rm.py:105 is literally '# TODO: Add time for checkpoint and restore', and the simulation branch at lines 251-295 advances a job by round_duration/job_iteration_time while charging nothing for launch, checkpoint or restore - yet Section 7 claims 'We ensure that the simulator can capture the job launch and preemption overheads and profile these overheads for the models we use (Table 2)' and reports 6.1% mean per-job JCT error against a real cluster (Figure 18). Section 4.2's explanation of the Figure 6 crossover is entirely about preemption cost - Tiresias 'causes long running jobs to suffer a large number of preemptions thus having longer average JCT at high load' - so if preemption is free in the model, the stated causal mechanism is untested. Section 8 ('Limitations of Simulation in Scheduling Research') concedes the gap.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Localized: a few hundred LOC across two files plus new profile fields, with the suspended/relaunch signal already plumbed through blox_manager. Reuses the committed sweep driver (simulator_runner/simulator.py) and the existing metrics JSON, so no new harness is needed. The sweep is pure CPU on 16 cores; the checkpoint profiling is minutes of single-GPU work on the A5000. Comfortably inside 10 weeks for 2-4 students.
addons.research_value_rationale: Blox's whole pitch is putting prior schedulers on a common, faithful footing; showing that the released simulator omits the exact cost to which the paper attributes its main comparative claim is a result a EuroSys reviewer would care about. Both outcomes teach something: if the crossover survives, the paper's conclusion is strengthened and now rests on a modelled mechanism rather than an unmodelled one; if it moves, the takeaways of Sections 4.2, 5.1 and 5.2 need restating - notably the 15% / 27.3% admission-control gains of Figures 12/13, which are precisely gains from reducing preemptions. The round-duration x checkpoint-cost plane is also a regime the paper never explores.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'papers citing Blox EuroSys 2024 deep learning scheduler simulator preemption overhead fidelity 2025'; 'GPU cluster scheduling simulator fidelity checkpoint preemption overhead modeling job completion time 2025 2026'. Injecting a restart penalty is standard in OTHER simulators - Pollux (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12260) injects a fixed 30 s checkpoint-restart delay per reallocation, and WiseShare (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.13088) validates its simulator to within ~5% of a testbed. Work citing Blox that was found (PAL, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.11919; WiseShare) cites it but does not audit its progress model. No paper found that re-derives Blox's own conclusions under a preemption-cost model.

addons.name: Make placement matter: placement-sensitive progress model plus the missing Tiresias placement policy
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that (i) applying the per-model placement_penalty already present in Blox's model zoo to simulated iteration time when a job spans multiple nodes and (ii) implementing the Tiresias skew-based placement policy plus an oracle 'Tiresias+' policy reproduces the qualitative conclusion of Figures 10 and 11 - consolidation wins at high load on fast-GPU/slow-network clusters and the oracle's lead grows with the fraction of placement-sensitive jobs - but that the magnitude of the gap is materially smaller than published once fragmentation feedback is modelled.
addons.mechanism: Set job['placement_preference'] in the workload generator from Model.placement_penalty; divide simulated iteration time by the penalty when a job's assigned GPUs span more than one Node_ID (available from cluster_state.gpu_df). Add TiresiasPlacement (skew heuristic over the profile) and OraclePlacement classes alongside JobPlacement, and wire a --placement-name switch into the drivers, which currently hard-fail on anything but 'Place' (blox_examples/blox_new_flow_multi_run.py:46-51). Fix the dead consolidation fallback at placement/placement.py:242 as part of the change. Sweep the placement-sensitive workload fraction 5/8 -> 8/8 as in Figure 11 and the load 1-8 jobs/hour as in Figure 10.
addons.motivating_evidence: placement_preference is READ at placement/placement.py:70,162 (and placement/first-gpu.py:81,173, placement/bebop.py:63) but a grep of workload/ shows it is never written, so place_consolidated is always False and every job takes the scattered path. placement_penalty is loaded into the model (workload/model.py:178) and attached to the job (workload/workload.py:190) but never reaches the simulated progress computation (blox/deployment/grpc_client_rm.py:251-264). placement/placement.py:242 assigns to a misspelled 'node_with_min_moRE_gpUs' instead of node_with_min_more_GPUs, making the only non-exact-match consolidation path dead code. And no Tiresias placement policy exists anywhere in placement/. Net effect: Section 4.3's case study - 'placement policies need to be guided by profiles on specific hardware they are deployed on, rather than using fixed heuristics' (Figures 10, 11) - has no reproducible code behind it.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Self-contained and well under 1k LOC; evaluated with the existing committed sweep on CPU only, no new harness and no GPU time. The one design decision - a defensible slowdown model for a job spanning >1 node - is already parameterised by the placement_penalty constants shipped in workload/models/*.py.
addons.research_value_rationale: It repairs and re-tests a published figure rather than opening new ground, and 'consolidation helps when the network is the bottleneck' is not a surprising headline - Tiresias and Synergy established it. It is genuinely valuable as a correctness contribution to the artifact and as necessary scaffolding for any placement-related follow-up (including A1's interaction with fragmentation), but a reviewer would call the result expected.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'GPU cluster scheduling network-sensitive placement consolidation Tiresias skew heuristic re-evaluation'; 'Blox scheduler toolkit extension new policy 2025 arXiv deep learning cluster scheduling reproduce'. Placement/network sensitivity is a well-worked area - GPU Cluster Scheduling for Network-Sensitive Deep Learning (https://arxiv.org/html/2401.16492v1) and WiseShare (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.13088v1) - so the idea itself is not novel. But no follow-up was found that supplies the missing placement machinery inside the Blox artifact or re-derives Figures 10/11.

addons.name: Cheap online policy selection to replace the brute-force Automatic Scheduler Synthesizer
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a contextual-bandit selector driven by cheap cluster-state features reaches within a few percent of the average JCT achieved by Blox's exhaustive simulate-every-combination synthesizer while cutting per-round selection cost by more than an order of magnitude, and that its advantage grows as the policy portfolio is scaled beyond the paper's 9 combinations.
addons.mechanism: Keep the outer loop of blox_examples/blox_new_flow_dynamic_policy.py and swap the oracle. Featurize each round from state already tracked - queue length, GPU demand/supply ratio, sliding-window arrival rate, short-job fraction, preemptions last round (all in cluster_state.cluster_stats and job_state.custom_metrics). Implement (a) a Thompson-sampling/UCB bandit over policy combinations with delayed JCT-based reward, (b) an epsilon-greedy baseline, (c) the paper's exhaustive lookahead as an upper bound, and (d) the best static policy as a lower bound. Instrument wall-clock per selection. Scale the portfolio from 9 to 25+ combinations by adding Srtf/Optimus/Tiresias crossed with more admission thresholds from admission_control/load_based_accept.py. Also implement the every-ten-rounds cadence the paper describes but the code does not.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 5.2 ends with the authors' own future work: 'In future we plan to extend this and rather than using simulation use a learning based approach to determine the policies to choose.' The released oracle is far more expensive than Section 5.2 describes: simulator_runner/predict_simulation.py takes a rounds_to_simulate argument and ignores it, instead looping 'while True: ... if len(job_state.active_jobs) == 0: break' (lines 112-218) - i.e. it drains ALL active jobs to completion for each itertools.product combination (lines 31-48), deep-copying ClusterState and JobState for every combination - and blox_examples/blox_new_flow_dynamic_policy.py:107 fires it every round ('if round_number % 1 == 0'), not every ten as the paper states. The paper reports the synthesizer's quality (Figures 14, 15, 20, 21) but never its cost, which is exactly the axis that decides whether the idea is deployable.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The selector itself is small, but an honest evaluation needs a new harness: portfolio-scaling experiments, per-round cost instrumentation, multiple traces (including the bursty Philly derivative of Section 5.2, which needs simulator_runner/simulator_dual_load.py), and repeated seeds because bandits are stochastic. Everything is CPU-only and fits the machine, but it is a lot of runs and it is cross-cutting rather than a single-file change.
addons.research_value_rationale: It is the paper's own named next step, it attacks a cost the paper never measured, and the portfolio-scaling regime is exactly where a modular toolkit's 'just compose more policies' promise either holds or breaks. A negative result - that a bandit cannot track a fast-changing trace and exhaustive lookahead is irreplaceable - would be an equally publishable finding about the synthesizer's premise, which makes both outcomes informative.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'automatic scheduler policy selection bandit reinforcement learning switching scheduling policies GPU cluster online 2025'; 'Blox scheduler toolkit extension new policy 2025'. There is substantial 2025 RL-for-GPU-scheduling work - hybrid learning/optimization dynamic scheduling, SoCC '25 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772052.3772257); defragmentation scheduling with DRL, SoCC '25 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3772052.3772242); network-contention-aware RL scheduling (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.20209) - but all of these LEARN a scheduling policy rather than SELECT among existing policy compositions at runtime, and none builds on or replaces Blox's synthesizer. Closest in spirit, not the same problem.

addons.name: Re-evaluate the schedulers under a transformer / LLM-fine-tuning workload mix
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing Blox's CNN/RNN-era model zoo with profiles measured from transformer fine-tuning jobs - which have longer, more uniform iteration times and far larger checkpoints - changes the JCT-versus-responsiveness ordering of FIFO/LAS/Tiresias/Optimus at a fixed load on Philly-Trace, and in particular erodes the benefit of preemption-heavy policies relative to Figure 6.
addons.mechanism: Profile 3-4 transformer fine-tuning workloads that fit 24 GB on the A5000 (BERT-base, GPT-2 small/medium, a 7B LoRA run, ViT): per-iteration time at the batch sizes the zoo uses, GPU memory, and checkpoint save/load time and size. Add them as ModelStats subclasses under workload/models/ following the workload/models/res18_1.py template, extend create_default_models and the task split in workload/model_zoo.py, and sweep the transformer fraction from 0% to 100% through the existing model_class_split knob (simulator_simple.py:40 -> workload/workload.py:70-75). Re-run the committed Figure 6/7 sweep in simulator_runner/simulator.py. Pairs naturally with A1, which supplies the checkpoint-cost channel through which large checkpoints actually bite.
addons.motivating_evidence: Sections 1 and 2.2 make workload evolution the paper's own motivation - 'popular DNN architectures evolve from CNNs to RNNs to Transformer-based models ... it becomes necessary to re-evaluate scheduler efficacy' and 'industry reports show that Transformer-based models such as BERT and DLRM now form a significant portion of the enterprise ML workload' - yet Table 2's zoo stops at ResNet/LSTM/CycleGAN/Recoder/A3C and the released zoo is the same: workload/model_zoo.py:190-196 lists alexnet, res18, res50, mobilenet, shufflenet, gnmt, transformer, lstm, deepspeech. The multi-GPU scaling numbers are hardcoded constants (workload/models/res18_1.py:19-29). The toolkit never exercised the transformer regime it argues for.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Profiling is cheap in GPU-hours and fits one 24 GB A5000 for single-GPU jobs; the simulation itself is CPU-only. The honest difficulty is that the zoo's throughput matrices are indexed by GPU count up to 16 (workload/model_zoo.py:181) while this machine has one GPU, so multi-GPU entries must either be extrapolated or the study restricted to the multigpu=False path - a real threat to validity that must be stated plainly rather than papered over.
addons.research_value_rationale: A well-motivated re-evaluation that the paper explicitly invites, and the outcome is not fully predictable. But it produces new numbers for an existing system rather than a new mechanism, and a reviewer may read 'modern models change the ranking' as the expected answer - it is a solid contribution rather than a surprising one.

scoop_check.details: Query: 're-evaluating DL cluster schedulers Tiresias Optimus on LLM fine-tuning workloads trace 2025 2026 GPU scheduling'. Plenty of 2025-26 LLM-serving and LLM-training scheduling work exists, and Saturn (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.01226) targets large-model training workloads, but no paper was found that re-runs the classic FIFO/LAS/Tiresias/Optimus comparison under a transformer-era workload mix on a common trace, and none that does so within Blox.

addons.name: In-process event-driven simulator core (and the churn-based scheduling question it unlocks)
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing Blox's two-process gRPC round loop with an in-process, event-driven core - one that advances simulated time to the next arrival, completion or lease expiry instead of ticking every 300 s - reduces wall-clock per simulated experiment by more than 10x while keeping per-job JCT within 1% of the current simulator, without changing any scheduling, placement or admission module.
addons.mechanism: Add a --simulate shim that substitutes direct method calls for BloxManager.rmserver and comm_node_manager so no socket is touched; replace the fixed 'simulator_time += args.round_duration' advance with an event queue keyed on arrivals, completions and lease expiries. Keep schedule()/place()/accept() signatures byte-identical so the existing policy modules run unmodified - which is itself the real test of whether Blox's abstraction boundary is as clean as Section 6.2 claims. Put the per-round copy.deepcopy of ClusterState/JobState in the placement wrapper (placement/placement.py:14-22) behind a flag. Validate by running the Figure 6 sweep on both cores and comparing JCT CDFs, then use the new core to measure the round-based versus churn-based JCT/responsiveness difference the paper defers.
addons.motivating_evidence: Readme.md:110 states 'The above experiment will take around 8hrs to run' for a single figure. Every simulated round crosses two gRPC hops (blox/blox_manager.py:87,125; simulator_simple.py:125-167) and deep-copies the whole cluster state and schedule (placement/placement.py:14-22). Section 8 explicitly defers the scientific question this unlocks: 'While our optimistic lease renewal can be used to support scheduling policies where the scheduling loop only kicks in on churn, we leave such investigation to the future.'
addons.feasibility_rationale: Cross-cutting: it touches the manager/RPC boundary that every driver goes through, and behavioural equivalence between the two cores must be demonstrated rather than assumed, which is itself a nontrivial experiment. No new hardware and no GPU time, so it fits the machine, but it is riskier than A1 or A2 and a divergence bug could eat weeks.
addons.research_value_rationale: Partly engineering - 'make the simulator faster' is not by itself a finding. It earns M because the toolkit is sold as a research accelerator, so 8 hours per figure is a first-class limitation, and because the event-driven core is the prerequisite for the churn-based-versus-round-based comparison the paper names as future work. A reviewer would want that comparison delivered alongside the speedup number, not the speedup alone.

scoop_check.details: Query: 'event-driven churn-based scheduling versus round-based DL cluster scheduler simulator speedup'. Event-driven cluster simulators are standard practice and the round-based/event-driven trade-off is discussed in the literature (ACM Queue on internet-scale cluster schedulers, https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3199609; round-based mechanisms for DL training, https://doi.org/10.3390/app14062349), so the technique is not novel. But nothing was found that does this inside Blox, or that quantifies the round-based versus churn-based JCT difference with Blox's abstractions held fixed.

risks: The released artifact is a subset of the paper: the Pollux, Themis and Synergy-Tune scheduling policies of Table 3 are absent (grep for pollux|themis yields only a comment at schedulers/optimus.py:31), so paper Figures 3, 5, 8 and 9 cannot be reproduced from this repo. Any plan depending on Pollux must budget for reimplementation - the paper itself charges 1157 LOC for it.

The released Tiresias is not the paper's Tiresias: schedulers/tiresias.py:42-52 builds the multi-queue discretized-LAS order into combine_across_all_list and then discards it, and the class defaults to num_queus=1, so it is behaviourally identical to LAS. The Figure 6 Tiresias curve may therefore not reproduce; writing a faithful discretized 2D-LAS is itself a possible sixth add-on.

Optimus crashes as released: blox/deployment/grpc_client_rm.py:268 reads self.optimus_scale_by_gpus, which is commented out at lines 232-243. The fix is mechanical but the commented values are an authorial guess that cannot be independently validated.

No artifact-evaluation badge was found. Searches of EuroSys '24 materials turned up nothing and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3627703.3629583 returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so this is 'not found', not 'confirmed absent'.

Dead and duplicated code raises the cost of every change: three near-copies of the workload tree (workload/, jobs/, helpers/ - only workload/ is live per simulator_simple.py:7), duplicate function definitions in blox/utils.py (lines 20/85 and 12/194), placement/consolidated.py using pd and find_free_GPUs without importing them, and the Gavel branch of placement/placement.py:137,142 referencing undefined jid and jobs_to_launch.

Stale dependency pins force a non-default environment: pandas < 2 because of gpu_df.append at blox/cluster_state.py:89, protobuf < 5 because of including_default_value_fields at blox/deployment/grpc_server_rm.py:42, which together force Python <= 3.10 in a conda env rather than the system 3.12. gRPC stubs are gitignored and the Makefile targets a directory that does not exist in the clone.

Runtime: the README budgets ~8 hours for one full Figure-6 sweep (Readme.md:110) and the published version has 27 configs. Parallelism across --simulator-rpc-port is the mitigation; the load/tracked-job scale-down is the fallback.

The real-cluster claims are out of reach: Figure 18 (32 GPUs on AWS) and Figure 19 (lease renewal to 256 GPUs) have no honest single-GPU scale-down on one A5000. Any hypothesis about lease-renewal scalability or simulator-versus-hardware fidelity is unavailable to this team, which is why add-on A1 targets internal consistency of the simulator rather than validation against real hardware.

Multi-GPU profiling gap: the model zoo's throughput matrices span 1-16 GPUs (workload/model_zoo.py:181) but this machine has one GPU, so any newly measured profile's multi-GPU entries are extrapolation and must be labelled as such - this bounds add-on A4 in particular.

Determinism is plausible but unverified: simulator_simple.py:90,320 fixes random.seed(1) per workload, yet the model-assignment path (workload/model_zoo.py:97-130) has seed-order-sensitive branches. Two identical runs should be diffed early before any comparative claim is made.

The bundled plotting path is broken - simulator_simple.py:182-287 expects filenames without the acceptance policy while blox/blox_manager.py:253 writes them with it, and line 281 references an undefined free_gpu - so all published figures must be re-plotted from the emitted JSON.
